\section{Methods: counterparty credit risk, CVA and the standardised approaches}
\label{sec:ccr}

A bank that holds a derivative with a counterparty is exposed to that counterparty twice. While the trade is alive its value to the bank
moves with the market, and if the counterparty fails to perform when the value is positive the bank loses part of it; if the value is
negative the bank owes it and loses nothing. Counterparty credit risk is therefore the credit risk of a quantity that is itself random,
the positive part of the value of a netting set at a future date. Three numbers describe it and they answer different questions. The
exposure at default is the figure a regulator multiplies by a risk weight to set capital. The expected exposure profile, averaged over
the first year, is the figure an internal model produces, with supervisory approval, in its place. The credit valuation adjustment
(CVA) is the price of the risk, the expected discounted loss from counterparty default over the whole life of the netting set; it
moves with the credit spread of the counterparty, and the Framework sets a capital charge for CVA risk apart from the charge for counterparty default
\citep{ccr:gregory2020,ccr:brigo2013,ccr:mar50}.

The regulation that governs the area is the Basel Framework in the chapters in force from 1 January 2023. The standardised approach to
counterparty credit risk, SA-CCR, sets the exposure at default of a netting set as $EAD=\alpha\,(RC+PFE)$ with $\alpha=1.4$, where
$RC$ is a replacement cost and $PFE$ a multiple of an add-on built from supervisory factors \citep{ccr:cre52}; five worked examples
of the chapter are published with their intermediate values \citep{ccr:cre99}. The internal model method sets the same quantity as
$\alpha$ times the effective expected positive exposure (EEPE) of a simulated profile, with a margin period of risk of at least ten
business days for a margined netting set, and requires the model to be backtested against realised market data at several horizons
\citep{ccr:cre53,ccr:bcbs185}. The capital charge for CVA risk is set, in its basic form, by the approach BA-CVA of the chapter on CVA
risk \citep{ccr:mar50}. Beside these the Framework fixes other formula-driven measures that a validator meets in the same department:
the floor that limits the benefit of internal models to a share of the standardised requirement \citep{ccr:rbc20,ccr:rbc90}, the
standardised measurement approach to operational risk \citep{ccr:ope25}, the liquidity coverage and net stable funding ratios
\citep{ccr:lcr,ccr:nsf}, and the sensitivities-based method of the market risk framework with its liquidity-horizon cascade
\citep{ccr:mar21,ccr:mar33}. Contraste implements the formulas of these chapters as calculators of the engine and reproduces the
official worked examples; it computes the measures and states no compliance claim.

Two methods of the product fall in this section. The first is the simulation of the exposure of an interest rate swap book with a
one-factor Hull-White model, with collateral, initial margin, CVA and wrong-way risk, and its backtest against the curves that were
realised (Section~\ref{sec:m20}). The second is the set of standardised calculators and their reproduction of the published examples
(Section~\ref{sec:m21}). The cases of the section are the six variants of case C12, run on a synthetic book of four USD swaps
priced on the US Treasury par yield curves from 1990 to 2025-09-30 \citep{ccr:treasurypar} with a counterparty spread proxy built
from the Treasury corporate bond curve \citep{ccr:treasuryhqm}. The variants ask one question each. The single swap asks how large the
exposure and the CVA of one ten-year payer swap are, and whether the engine's expected exposure equals that of an independent engine,
ORE 1.8.17.0 \citep{ccr:ore}, within the Monte Carlo error. The netting set asks how much of the sum of the single-trade exposures
netting removes. Two variants with a credit support annex and a margin period of risk of 10 and 20 business days ask how much
variation margin cuts the exposure and how the answer changes with the period. The variant with initial margin asks what a dynamic
initial margin removes from the expected exposure and what the standardised approach credits for it. The wrong-way risk variant asks
how the CVA changes when the default intensity of the counterparty moves with the value of the portfolio. All six share one backtest:
would the simulated distributions of the book value and of the short rate have held against the Treasury curves published later?
The book is synthetic and its numbers are not those of any bank; the curves are real.

\subsection{Exposure and CVA by one-factor Hull-White simulation, with collateral, initial margin and wrong-way risk}
\label{sec:m20}

\subsubsection{The short-rate model and its fit to today's curve}

The value of an interest rate swap at a future date depends on the whole curve at that date, so an exposure model needs a law for the
curve. Contraste uses the Hull-White one-factor model \citep{ccr:hullwhite1990}, the standard Gaussian short-rate model whose bond
prices are affine and whose option prices have closed forms. The short rate is the sum of a deterministic fitting function and an
Ornstein-Uhlenbeck state,
\begin{equation}
r_t=\varphi(t)+x_t,\qquad \mathrm{d}x_t=-a\,x_t\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma\,\mathrm{d}W_t,\quad x_0=0,\qquad
\varphi(t)=f(0,t)+\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\sigma\,(1-e^{-at})}{a}\right]^{2},
\label{eq:ccr-hw}
\end{equation}
where $a>0$ is the speed of mean reversion in units of 1/year, $\sigma>0$ is the volatility of the short rate in units of
1/$\sqrt{\text{year}}$, $W$ is a standard Brownian motion under the risk-neutral measure, and $f(0,t)$ is the instantaneous forward rate
of today's curve. The choice of $\varphi$ is the fitting parameter of the QuantLib implementation \citep{ccr:quantlib}; it makes the model
reprice every discount factor $P(0,T)$ of the curve exactly. The equivalent form $\mathrm{d}r=(\theta(t)-a\,r)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma\,\mathrm{d}W$
with $\theta(t)=\partial_t f(0,t)+a f(0,t)+\frac{\sigma^2}{2a}(1-e^{-2at})$ follows by algebra and is the textbook statement
\citep{ccr:brigomercurio2006}; the engine uses the first form, which avoids the derivative of the forward curve. The discount factor
of a zero-coupon bond maturing at $T$, seen at $t$, is affine in the short rate,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
P(t,T)&=A(t,T)\,e^{-B(t,T)\,r_t},\qquad B(t,T)=\frac{1-e^{-a(T-t)}}{a},\\
A(t,T)&=\frac{P(0,T)}{P(0,t)}\exp\!\Big[B\,f(0,t)-\frac{\sigma^2}{4a}\big(1-e^{-2at}\big)B^2\Big],
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-bond}
\end{equation}
with $B(t,t)=0$ and $A(t,t)=1$; for $a$ below the square root of machine precision the code uses $B=T-t$, so the limit $a\to0$ needs no
division. Two identities guard the transcription. At $t=0$ and $r=\varphi(0)=f(0,0)$ the factor $e^{-Br}$ cancels the forward term of
$A$ and the price equals $P(0,T)$ for every $T$ of the curve and every pair $(a,\sigma)$; and the discounted bond prices are martingales
under the simulated measure, $E[e^{-\int_0^t r_s\mathrm{d}s}P(t,T;r_t)]=P(0,T)$ at every date.

The state is simulated by its exact transition rather than by an Euler step. On a grid $0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_K$ with steps
$\Delta_i=t_i-t_{i-1}$,
\begin{equation}
x_{t_i}=x_{t_{i-1}}\,e^{-a\Delta_i}+\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1-e^{-2a\Delta_i}}{2a}}\;z_i,\qquad z_i\sim N(0,1),
\label{eq:ccr-exact}
\end{equation}
so that the law of the path does not depend on the step \citep{ccr:brigo2008}. The antithetic pairing sets path $i+P/2$ equal to minus path
$i$, which fixes the sample mean of the state at zero. The
numeraire is the bank account $N(t)=\exp\int_0^t r_s\,\mathrm{d}s$. The integral of the deterministic part is evaluated in closed form,
$\int_0^t\varphi=-\ln P(0,t)+\frac{\sigma^2}{2a^2}\big[t-\tfrac{2(1-e^{-at})}{a}+\tfrac{1-e^{-2at}}{2a}\big]$, and only the state is
integrated by the trapezoid rule on the grid. A trapezoid on $r$ itself misses $\int\varphi$ by an amount that depends on the grid, because the
forward of a zero curve jumps at the pillars of the curve, and that bias would enter every discounted exposure and every CVA; with
$\sigma=0$ the closed form gives $1/N(t)=P(0,t)$ to $10^{-12}$ on any grid.

\subsubsection{Calibration of the mean reversion and the volatility}

The curve fixes $\varphi$ but not $(a,\sigma)$. Contraste takes them from the history of one short-rate proxy, the 3~month zero rate bootstrapped
from the Treasury par curve, by the regression of the exact transition. Writing $x_{t_i}=c+b\,x_{t_{i-1}}+\delta\,\epsilon_i$ with $\epsilon_i$ standard
normal and $\Delta$ the sampling step in years, the least-squares estimates $(\hat c,\hat b,\hat\delta)$ map to the model by
\begin{equation}
a=-\frac{\ln b}{\Delta},\qquad \theta=\frac{c}{1-b},\qquad
\sigma=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{\dfrac{(b^{2}-1)\,\Delta}{2\ln b}}},
\label{eq:ccr-ar1}
\end{equation}
which is the discretisation of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process in \citet{ccr:brigo2008}. The standard errors of $a$ and $\sigma$ follow by the delta method from the
ordinary least squares standard error of $b$ and the normal-theory error $\delta/\sqrt{2(m-2)}$ of the residual spread, with $m$ pairs, taken as independent. Three
conditions protect the estimate. Only observations strictly before the calibration date enter, so a backtest cannot see the future; fewer than
three years of history raise an error \citep[CRE53.51]{ccr:cre53}; and a regression with $b\notin(0,1)$, which is not mean-reverting, raises an error. The fit is of the physical
measure, whereas the drift $\varphi$ is risk-neutral, so the history supplies $a$ and $\sigma$ only. In Contraste the expanding window starts at the first
Treasury file of 1990 and ends the day before the date; rolling windows of five and ten years were tried first and refused, because the regression is not
mean-reverting at about a third of the dates. At the curve date of the book, \ccrCurveDate, the estimates are $a=\ccrHwA$ per year with standard error
\ccrHwASe{} and $\sigma=\ccrHwSigma$ with standard error \ccrHwSigmaSe, from \ccrNObs{} daily observations between \ccrSampleStart{} and \ccrSampleEnd{}
(\ccrHistYears{} years). The estimates over the \ccrCalDates{} monthly backtest dates range from \ccrCalAMin{} to \ccrCalAMax{} for $a$ and from \ccrCalSigmaMin{}
to \ccrCalSigmaMax{} for $\sigma$ (Figure~\ref{fig:ccr-calibration}); the first date has \ccrCalFirstYears{} years of history and the estimate $a=\ccrCalFirstA$.

\subsubsection{Closed forms: the bond option and the Jamshidian swaption}

Two options have closed forms in the model and both are needed. For an option expiring at $T$ on a zero-coupon bond maturing at $S$ with strike $K$ quoted as a bond price,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_p&=\sigma\,B(T,S)\sqrt{\frac{1-e^{-2aT}}{2a}},\qquad h=\frac{\ln\frac{P(0,S)}{K\,P(0,T)}}{\sigma_p}+\frac{\sigma_p}{2},\\
\mathrm{ZBC}&=P(0,S)\,N(h)-K\,P(0,T)\,N(h-\sigma_p),
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-zbo}
\end{equation}
where $N$ is the standard normal distribution function and $\sigma_p$ is the standard deviation of the log bond price at the expiry; the put follows from put-call parity,
$\mathrm{ZBC}-\mathrm{ZBP}=P(0,S)-K\,P(0,T)$. A European swaption on the swap that remains after the expiry $T_e$, with fixed payment times $T_i$, coupon amounts $c_i$ and the nominal $N$ added to
the last coupon, is a portfolio of such options, by the decomposition of \citet{ccr:jamshidian1989}: because every bond price is decreasing in the short rate, the payoff is exercised
exactly when the short rate is above the critical rate $r^\ast$ for a payer swaption, whose payoff $(N-\sum_ic_iP(T_e,T_i))^+$ is positive when the bond prices are low,
and below it for a receiver swaption, where $r^\ast$ solves
\begin{equation}
N-\sum_i c_i\,P(T_e,T_i;r^\ast)=0,\qquad \text{Swaption}=\sum_i c_i\,\mathrm{ZBO}\big(K_i=P(T_e,T_i;r^\ast)\big),
\label{eq:ccr-jam}
\end{equation}
a put on each coupon bond for a payer swaption and a call for a receiver swaption. The root is found by Brent's method on $[-10,10]$ to $10^{-12}$ so that the payer-minus-receiver parity
with the forward swap value holds to $10^{-9}$. Both formulas are transcribed from the QuantLib source \citep{ccr:quantlib}; the journal derivations were not re-read as papers, and the engine is
held to the library numerically instead (Section~\ref{sec:results-ccr}). The forms matter for two reasons: they price the single-swap exposure analytically (below), and they give an
independent check of the simulation that does not use Monte Carlo at all.

\subsubsection{The value of a swap along a path}

A swap in the book has notional $N$, a fixed rate $K$, a direction (the payer pays the fixed rate), a start, a maturity and a fixed frequency; the floating leg resets on the same dates on the single
curve of the case, with no spread. With fixed payment times $T_i$ and accrual fractions $\tau_i$, the fixed coupons are $c_i=N K\tau_i$. At a reset date $T_j$ the floating coupon
$N\tau L_j$ with $L_j=\big(1/P(T_j,T_{j+1})-1\big)/\tau$ is fixed and paid at $T_{j+1}$. Only the flows after the valuation date $t$ are valued, which is the sticky-date convention of the close-out, and the
floating leg is
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
V^{\mathrm{float}}(t)&=N\big(P(t,T_{0}')-P(t,T_n)\big),\quad t\text{ on or before a reset, }T_0'\text{ the next reset},\\
V^{\mathrm{float}}(t)&=N\tau L_j\,P(t,T_{j+1})+N\big(P(t,T_{j+1})-P(t,T_n)\big),\quad T_j<t<T_{j+1},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-float}
\end{equation}
where the second case needs the fixing $L_j$ of the same path; its absence is an error and is never approximated. The value to the bank of a payer swap is $V^{\mathrm{float}}-\sum_i c_i P(t,T_i)$ over the remaining payments and a receiver swap has the opposite
sign. The par rate of a swap starting at $s$ and maturing at $T$ is $(P(0,s)-P(0,T))/\sum_i\tau_i P(0,T_i)$, and a swap at its par rate has value zero at the start. The netting-set value is the sum of the swap values, never the sum of their positive parts. A check that depends on no formula
of this subsection is the martingale property of the discounted value: it is not a martingale by itself, because a flow paid at a date leaves the portfolio, but its mean equals the value today minus the present value of the flows paid at or before the date.

In Contraste the book is four swaps with semiannual fixed legs (Table~\ref{tab:ccr-book}); the fixed rate of each is the par yield of its maturity on \ccrCurveDate, rounded to 10 basis points, so the book is close to par but not at par, and its value at the valuation
date is \ccrVNetting{} USD. The report grid has \ccrGridPoints{} dates: monthly to one year, quarterly to three years and half-yearly to nine and a half years, so that every reset falls on a grid date; at ten years every exposure is zero.

\subsubsection{Exposure measures}

For a netting set of value $V(t)$ and numeraire $N(t)$, the expected exposure and the expected negative exposure are
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{EE}(t)=E\!\left[\frac{\max(V(t),0)}{N(t)}\right],\qquad \mathrm{ENE}(t)=E\!\left[\frac{\max(-V(t),0)}{N(t)}\right],
\label{eq:ccr-ee}
\end{equation}
the first the exposure to the counterparty and the second the bank's own, reported as a positive number \citep{ccr:ore}. The Basel style measure is undiscounted, $\mathrm{EE}_B(t)=E[\max(V(t),0)]$; in the simulation measure the two
are related by $\mathrm{EE}_B(t)=\mathrm{EE}(t)/P(0,t)$, which is the expectation in the $t$-forward measure. Each profile comes with its Monte Carlo standard error, the sample standard deviation over the square root of the number of paths $P$. The potential future exposure at level
$q$ is the positive part of the $q$-quantile of the value, and netting is stated on the sum of the values,
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{PFE}_q(t)=\Big(\inf\{x:F_t(x)\ge q\}\Big)^{+},\qquad \max\Big(\sum_s v_s,0\Big)\le\sum_s\max(v_s,0),
\label{eq:ccr-pfe}
\end{equation}
where $F_t$ is the distribution function of the value; the standard error of the quantile is estimated by the bootstrap of the paths with a fixed seed. The regulatory measures of the internal model method are
the running maximum of the expected exposure, its time average over the first year and the effective maturity \citep{ccr:cre53},
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{EEE}_{t_k}&=\max(\mathrm{EEE}_{t_{k-1}},\mathrm{EE}_{t_k}),\qquad
\mathrm{EEPE}=\sum_{t_k\le\min(1,\,T_{\max})}\mathrm{EEE}_{t_k}\,\Delta t_k,\\
M&=\min\!\left(5,\ \frac{\sum_{t_k\le1}\mathrm{EEE}_k\Delta t_kdf_k+\sum_{t_k>1}\mathrm{EE}_k\Delta t_kdf_k}{\sum_{t_k\le1}\mathrm{EEE}_k\Delta t_kdf_k}\right),
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-eff}
\end{equation}
with $\mathrm{EEE}_{t_0}$ the current exposure, $T_{\max}$ the longest maturity and $df_k$ the discount factors; when every contract matures within the year the effective maturity is 1, and the cap is five years. In Contraste the
effective EE starts from zero and the current exposure is the replacement cost of the SA-CCR block. The regulatory exposure at default under the model is $1.4$ times the EEPE, and the engine states the measures and
applies no multiplier; the factor 1.4 is applied where Contraste compares the measures (Section~\ref{sec:results-ccr}). The expectation of the model is taken in the risk-neutral measure of the simulation; the footnote of CRE53.12 states that the expectation should in theory be under
the actual distribution and that supervisors do not mandate which distribution is used, so the profiles are those of the model's measure and the PFE is a quantile in that measure.

\subsubsection{The analytic profile of one swap}

The expected exposure of a single swap has an analytic expression that does not use the simulation, which makes it an independent check of the simulated profile. Without collateral, $E[\max(V(t),0)/N(t)]$ is by risk-neutral pricing the price today of a European option that pays $\max(V(t),0)$ at
$t$, that is a swaption expiring at $t$ on the remaining swap, a payer swaption for a payer swap and a receiver swaption for a receiver swap. Dividing by the discount factor to the expiry moves the expectation to the $t$-forward measure:
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{EE}_B(t)=\frac{\mathrm{Swaption}(0;t)}{P(0,t)},
\label{eq:ccr-analytic}
\end{equation}
with the swaption of Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-jam} and the flows at or before $t$ excluded. The identity holds on the reset dates of the swap only, because between two resets the remaining swap carries a fixed current coupon and is not a forward-starting swap; the engine refuses a date that is neither a reset nor at or after the maturity. This is a derivation of the
engine's documentation from the definition of exposure and not a result transcribed from a paper. It holds in the risk-neutral measure of the model and says nothing about the real-world exposure.

\subsubsection{Collateral, the margin period of risk and initial margin}

With a credit support annex the bank holds collateral against the value. At a margin date $t_m$ the credit support amount depends on the netting-set value $\mathrm{NPV}$, the independent amount $IA$ (positive when received) and the thresholds $Th_{rec}$ and $Th_{pay}$, and the delivery amount
is the shortfall of the held collateral $C$ and the outstanding calls $M$ against it, if it exceeds the minimum transfer amount $MTA$ \citep{ccr:ore}:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{CSA}&=\begin{cases}\max(0,\mathrm{NPV}+IA-Th_{rec}), & \mathrm{NPV}+IA\ge0\\ \min(0,\mathrm{NPV}+IA+Th_{pay}), & \mathrm{NPV}+IA<0,\end{cases}\\
\Delta&=\mathrm{CSA}-C-M,\qquad D=\begin{cases}\Delta,&|\Delta|\ge MTA\\0,&|\Delta|<MTA.\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-csa}
\end{equation}
Collateral does not remove the exposure, because after a default the bank closes out the netting set only after a margin period of risk $\tau$ during which no margin is received. The residual exposure at the default time $t$ is the close-out value $V(t)$ against the collateral that could last be received,
$C(t-\tau)$, and it is positive even with zero thresholds and zero minimum transfer amount:
\begin{equation}
E_C(t)=\max\big(V(t)-C(t-\tau),\,0\big).
\label{eq:ccr-resid}
\end{equation}
This is the close-out formulation of ORE, with an auxiliary grid offset from the main grid by $\tau$: the main grid values feed the balance and the offset grid gives $V$ \citep{ccr:ore,ccr:hullwhite2012}. The close-out value is the sticky-date value, in which the market moves from the default date to the close-out date and the portfolio does not age; the alternative
that includes the flows of the window, with its exposure spikes, is not implemented, and neither is the legacy lagged approach. The margin period of risk is stated in business days, 250 to the year, and its floor in CRE53.24 is 10 business days, raised to 20 for a netting set with more than 5,000 trades, illiquid collateral or an OTC derivative that
cannot be easily replaced; more than two margin call disputes in two quarters double the period (CRE53.25) and remargining with a periodicity of $N$ days adds $N-1$ days to the floor (CRE53.26) \citep{ccr:cre53}.

Initial margin enters through a regression. With the netting-set value $\mathrm{NPV}$, the margin period $\Delta_m$ in calendar days and the cash flows $F$ of the period, the change in value over the period is $X(t)=\mathrm{NPV}(t+\Delta_m)+F(t,t+\Delta_m)-\mathrm{NPV}(t)$ and the dynamic initial margin is
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{DIM}(t)=\Phi^{-1}(q)\,\sqrt{E_t[X^2]-E_t^2[X]}\;\sqrt{\frac{H}{\Delta_m}},\qquad E_t[X^2]\approx c_0+c_1v+\dots+c_nv^n,
\label{eq:ccr-dim}
\end{equation}
where $\Phi^{-1}(q)$ is the normal quantile of the confidence level, $H$ the horizon of the margin in calendar days, and the conditional second moment is regressed over the Monte Carlo paths on a polynomial of the netting-set value $v$ in the manner of the least-squares regression of \citet{ccr:longstaff2001}, a regression the ORE guide
describes in that spirit \citep{ccr:ore}. The margin reduces the exposure path by path, $E=\max(E_{VM}-\mathrm{DIM},0)$, and applies only together with variation margin. It is a regression proxy and never the ISDA SIMM, whose methodology carries a notice that it cannot be used, revised or
distributed except for a participant's own commercial transactions \citep{ccr:simm}; the SIMM risk weights are not reimplemented. The margin period timelines of \citet{ccr:andersen2017}, with remedies, suspension rights and the time to exercise them, are not modelled. The parameters of Contraste are a threshold of zero, a minimum transfer amount of \ccrMta{} USD
and an independent amount of zero; the margin period is 10 business days for the first margined variant, the floor, and 20 for the second, the value CRE53.24 prescribes for large or illiquid netting sets; the margin quantile is \ccrImQuantile{} with a regression of order two and a horizon equal to the margin period of 14 calendar days.

\subsubsection{CVA, DVA and wrong-way risk}

The counterparty's default probabilities come from a credit curve. With a spread $s$ per year and a loss given default $LGD$ the credit triangle gives the survival probability and the default probability of a bucket; the unilateral, discretised CVA and DVA with independence between exposure and default are
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
S(t)&=\exp\!\Big[-\frac{s\,t}{LGD}\Big],\qquad \mathrm{PD}(t_{i-1},t_i)=S(t_{i-1})-S(t_i),\\
\mathrm{CVA}&=LGD\sum_i\mathrm{PD}(t_{i-1},t_i)\,\mathrm{EE}(t_i),\\
\mathrm{DVA}&=LGD_B\sum_i\mathrm{PD}_B(t_{i-1},t_i)\,\mathrm{ENE}(t_i),
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-cva}
\end{equation}
with the discounted expectations $\mathrm{EE}$ and $\mathrm{ENE}$ of Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-ee}, and the subscript $B$ for the bank's own curve and loss given default. This is the advanced discretisation of ORE; the simple bilateral value is $\mathrm{CVA}-\mathrm{DVA}$, and the consistent first-to-default form, in which each term is
multiplied by the survival probability of the other party, is not implemented \citep{ccr:brigo2013,ccr:gregory2020}. CVA is a cost, DVA a benefit; CVA is exactly zero at a zero spread. For given default probabilities it is linear in the loss given default and in the exposure; with the probabilities implied from a fixed spread by the credit triangle above, the loss given default cancels to first order, because $\mathrm{PD}(t_{i-1},t_i)\approx s\,(t_i-t_{i-1})/LGD$, and CVA is then linear in the spread and in the exposure. The counterparty spread of the base case is the Treasury corporate (HQM) spot curve minus the Treasury zero curve of the same month end, an AAA to A market spread that is a floor for
lower ratings; a negative difference is set to zero and counted, and none was. The synthetic flat spread of 0.0125 is carried as a sensitivity only. The loss given default is \ccrCpLgd{} and the bank's own spread is \ccrBankSpread, both conventions.

Wrong-way risk is the dependence of the default intensity on the exposure. \citet{ccr:hullwhite2012} model the hazard rate as an exponential function of the portfolio value $w$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
h(t)&=\exp\big[a(t)+b\,w(t)\big],\qquad \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\exp\Big(-\sum_{i=1}^{k}h_{ij}\Delta t_i\Big)=\exp\Big(-\frac{s_kt_k}{LGD}\Big)\ \ (k=1,2,\dots),\\
\mathrm{CVA}&=LGD\sum_i\frac{1}{m}\sum_j\mathrm{PD}_{ij}E_{ij},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-wwr}
\end{equation}
where $b$ in units of 1/USD million measures the wrong-way ($b>0$) or right-way ($b<0$) dependence, $a(t)$ is a function of time, $h_{ij}$ is the hazard on path $j$ at step $i$, $m$ the number of paths, $s_k$ the spread to maturity $t_k$, $\mathrm{PD}_{ij}$ the path-wise default probability of the bucket and $E_{ij}$ the discounted positive exposure.
The function $a(t)$ is calibrated step by step so that the average survival over the paths equals the survival implied by the spread, which keeps the unconditional default probability of the counterparty unchanged and moves only its dependence on the value (Algorithm~\ref{alg:ccr-wwr}). The noise term of the paper's equation (8)
makes little difference unless it is large relative to $w$, and the working model is the form of Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-wwr}. With $b=0$ the hazard does not depend on the path and the value equals the independent CVA computed on the same paths, bit for bit. The algorithm is checked on the three-path example of the paper's Appendix, whose printed values are
$a(t_1^\ast)=-6.9128$ and $a(t_2^\ast)=-7.8509$ and which the engine reproduces to $2\times10^{-4}$ for $a$ and $10^{-5}$ for $h$, against the values recomputed from the printed equations to $5\times10^{-6}$ and $5\times10^{-7}$; the paper's own CVA tables are for a foreign exchange forward
and are not reproduced for a swap. Contraste sweeps $b$ over the grid in Table~\ref{tab:ccr-wwr}.

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{Calibration of the deterministic part $a(t)$ of the wrong-way hazard and the CVA with dependence (variant \texttt{wrong-way-risk}).}
\label{alg:ccr-wwr}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require simulated portfolio values $w_{ij}$ and discounted exposures $E_{ij}$ on $m$ paths and $K$ dates, target survival $S^\ast_k=\exp(-s_kt_k/LGD)$, steps $\Delta t_i$, dependence $b$, loss given default $LGD$
\State $H_{j}\leftarrow0$ for every path $j$ \Comment{accumulated hazard}
\For{$k=1,\dots,K$}
  \State find $a_k$ by a root search on $\frac{1}{m}\sum_j\exp\big(-H_j-e^{a_k+b\,w_{kj}}\Delta t_k\big)-S^\ast_k=0$ \Comment{refuse a target that nonnegative hazards cannot reach}
  \State $h_{kj}\leftarrow e^{a_k+b\,w_{kj}}$; $\quad S_{kj}\leftarrow\exp\big(-H_j-h_{kj}\Delta t_k\big)$; $\quad H_j\leftarrow H_j+h_{kj}\Delta t_k$
\EndFor
\State $\mathrm{PD}_{kj}\leftarrow S_{k-1,j}-S_{kj}$ with $S_{0j}=1$; $\quad\mathrm{CVA}\leftarrow LGD\sum_k\frac{1}{m}\sum_j\mathrm{PD}_{kj}E_{kj}$; standard error from the spread of $\sum_k\mathrm{PD}_{kj}E_{kj}$ over paths
\Ensure $a_1,\dots,a_K$, hazards $h_{kj}$, CVA with its Monte Carlo error, largest calibration error $\max_k\big|\frac1m\sum_jS_{kj}-S^\ast_k\big|$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\subsubsection{The exposure backtest}

A model that produces an exposure distribution is tested by comparing its distribution with what happened. BCBS~185 defines the backtest of a counterparty credit risk model as the quantitative comparison of its forecasts with realised values, requires several horizons including those of typical margin periods and one year, and a calibration that uses no data after the initialisation date; CRE53.33 repeats the
requirement \citep{ccr:bcbs185,ccr:cre53}. Contraste follows it. On each month end from 2000-01 the model is calibrated on the observations before that date (Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-ar1}), fitted to that date's curve, and the book is originated at par on that curve. The paths are simulated to six horizons, 10 and 20 business days (14 and 28 calendar days) and
1, 3, 6 and 12 months; the realised value of the book at each horizon is the engine's swap value of the remaining swaps on the curve actually published at the end of the horizon. For $P$ simulated values $\hat r^{(1)}<\dots<\hat r^{(P)}$ and a realised value $r$ the probability integral transform and the Anderson-Darling distance of the $n$ transforms
$F(x_1),\dots,F(x_n)$ ordered increasingly are \citep{ccr:formenti2015}
\begin{equation}
F(r)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{P+2},&r<\hat r^{(1)}\\[2pt]\frac{i+1}{P+2},&\hat r^{(i)}<r<\hat r^{(i+1)}\\[2pt]\frac{P+1}{P+2},&r>\hat r^{(P)}\end{cases}\qquad
W^2=-n-\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{2k-1}{n}\Big[\ln F(x_k)+\ln\big(1-F(x_{n+1-k})\big)\Big].
\label{eq:ccr-pit}
\end{equation}
If the model matches the realised values the transforms are uniform. The upper-tail values of $W^2$ for independent transforms are \ccrIidFive{} at 5 percent and \ccrIidOne{} at 1 percent, but overlapping horizons make the transforms dependent, so the critical values are obtained by simulating the whole backtest under the model, at the same dates and with the same overlapping horizons,
\ccrCriticalCount{} times, and the effective sample size of the transforms is reported. It is computed from $z_i=\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{PIT}_i)$ and its autocorrelations $\rho_k$ with Bartlett weights, a convention of the contract and not a backtesting standard:
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{ESS}=\frac{n}{1+2\sum_{k=1}^{L}\big(1-\frac{k}{L+1}\big)\rho_k},\qquad L=\lfloor n^{1/3}\rfloor,\qquad 1\le\mathrm{ESS}\le n.
\label{eq:ccr-ess}
\end{equation}
The count of exceedances of the PFE forecast by the realised value is a secondary row, because exception counting often assumes independence and the data overlap (paragraph 27 of BCBS~185). Its test is the Kupiec likelihood ratio of unconditional coverage \citep{market:kupiec1995} for $N$ dates, $x$ exceedances and expected rate $p=1-q$,
\begin{equation}
LR=-2\ln\!\big[(1-p)^{N-x}p^{x}\big]+2\ln\!\Big[\big(1-\tfrac{x}{N}\big)^{N-x}\big(\tfrac{x}{N}\big)^{x}\Big],\qquad p\text{-value}=\Pr[\chi^2_1>LR],
\label{eq:ccr-kupiec}
\end{equation}
which is green at $p\ge0.05$, amber below 0.05 and red below 0.01 (the levels the exposure backtest function fixes for itself). The market battery of the previous section turns the same test amber below \mkAmberAlpha{} and red below \mkRedAlpha{}, the levels its tests take as parameters; the two batteries use different screening levels, and a colour is read against the levels of its own battery. The risk factor, the 3~month zero rate, is backtested beside the book, simulated as $-\ln P(t,t+0.25)/0.25$ from the bond price and realised from the published 3~month par yield; the exposure operator is not applied to market data. Three sub-windows, before 2008, 2008 to 2019 and from 2020,
are reported apart. The settings of Contraste are \ccrBtDates{} dates, \ccrBacktestPaths{} paths per date and \ccrBtHorizons{} horizons.

\subsubsection{Parameters, assumptions, procedure, complexity and implementation}

The parameters of the method, with their values and status in Contraste, are in Table~\ref{tab:ccr-params}. Those estimated from data are $a$ and $\sigma$; every other value is a convention of the synthetic book, the credit support annex, the counterparty curve or the test, and the artifacts label each one. The choices that carry weight were made as follows:
the number of paths, \ccrPathCount, with the seed \ccrSeed, so that a bake writes the same bytes on any device; the margin period of 10 business days because it is the supervisory floor; the expanding calibration window because shorter windows are not mean-reverting; and the simulated critical values because the transforms of overlapping horizons are dependent. The assumptions are those of the model: one factor, a constant $a$ and a constant $\sigma$, a European
swaption, a single curve with no basis, swaps of the same fixed and floating frequency with no stub and no amortisation, immediate settlement of margin at each report date with the lag represented by the close-out grid, and the risk-neutral measure for the expectation.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\caption{The cost in time and memory of each step of Algorithm~\ref{alg:ccr-exposure}, derived from its loops, in the number of paths $P$, report dates $K$, swaps $S$ with $n_s$ payments each, regression order $d$ and payments $n$ of the swap under a swaption.}
\label{tab:ccr-cost}
\begin{tabular}{p{4.2cm}p{4.2cm}p{4.2cm}}
\toprule
Step & Cost (own analysis) & Memory \\
\midrule
state paths and bank account & $O(PK)$ & $O(PK)$ \\
swap values on the grid & $O\big(PK\sum_sn_s\big)$ & $O(SPK)$ \\
EE, ENE with errors & $O(PK)$ & $O(K)$ \\
PFE by sorting each date & $O(KP\log P)$ & $O(P)$ \\
credit support amount and delivery & $O(PK)$ & $O(PK)$ \\

CVA and DVA & $O(K)$ & $O(K)$ \\
Jamshidian swaption at one date & $O(In)$ for $I$ root iterations & $O(n)$ \\

\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{The exposure, margin and CVA of a netting set along Hull-White paths (cases of C12; one simulation feeds all variants).}
\label{alg:ccr-exposure}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require swaps, curve $P(0,\cdot)$ and $f(0,\cdot)$, $(a,\sigma)$, report grid, paths $P$, seed, CSA terms, margin period $\tau$, margin quantile $q$, credit curves, loss given default
\State build the simulation grid as the union of the report grid, the reset dates and the close-out dates $t_k+\tau$
\State draw the antithetic states by Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-exact}; set $r=\varphi+x$ and compute the bank account $N(t)$ with the closed-form integral of $\varphi$
\State value every swap at every report date and close-out date by Equations~\ref{eq:ccr-bond} and~\ref{eq:ccr-float}; sum over swaps to $V_k$ and $V^{c}_k$
\If{the netting set has a CSA}
  \State follow Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-csa} from a zero balance along the report grid to obtain $C_k$; set $E_k\leftarrow\max(V^{c}_k-C_k,0)$ by Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-resid}
\Else \State $E_k\leftarrow\max(V_k,0)$ \EndIf
\If{initial margin applies} \State regress $X^2$ on a polynomial of $V_k$, form $\mathrm{DIM}_k$ by Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-dim} and set $E_k\leftarrow\max(E_k-\mathrm{DIM}_k,0)$ \EndIf
\State compute $\mathrm{EE}$, $\mathrm{ENE}$ with errors, $\mathrm{PFE}_q$, the effective EE, $\mathrm{EEPE}$ and $M$ (Equations~\ref{eq:ccr-ee}, \ref{eq:ccr-pfe}, \ref{eq:ccr-eff})
\State convert the spread curves to survival by the credit triangle and sum Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-cva} to obtain CVA and DVA with their errors
\Ensure profiles with errors, EEPE, effective maturity, CVA, DVA
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

The procedure is Algorithm~\ref{alg:ccr-exposure}. Its costs are in Table~\ref{tab:ccr-cost}; they are derived here from the structure of the loops and are not measured. The valuation of the swaps dominates for a large book, the regression of the margin adds a cubic term in the order only, and the memory is the matrix of values of $P$ paths and $K$ dates. The simulation is deterministic given the seed:
every function is pure, takes a seed where it has randomness and uses \ccrfn{numpy.random.default_rng}, and the thread counts of the bake are pinned so that the summation order does not change.

The implementation is the package \ccrfn{riskvalidation} 1.1.0 on PyPI, modules \ccrfn{riskvalidation.ccr.hw1f}, \ccrfn{swaps}, \ccrfn{exposure}, \ccrfn{collateral} and \ccrfn{cva} for the model, the swaps, the measures, the margin and the adjustment (Table~\ref{tab:ccr-modules}), and \ccrfn{riskvalidation.validation.ccr} for the test battery; the product's pipeline modules \ccrfn{pipeline/cases/c12/exposure.py}, \ccrfn{credit.py},
\ccrfn{regulatory.py}, \ccrfn{backtest.py}, \ccrfn{reconcile.py} and \ccrfn{variant.py} sequence the engine calls for the six variants and never compute a measure themselves. The module \ccrfn{pipeline/cases/c12/ore.py} runs ORE 1.8.17.0 natively from its wheel with \ccrOreSamples{} antithetic samples, a linear Gauss-Markov model carrying the Hull-White $a$ and $\sigma$ without calibration, 30/360 time and monthly scenario tenors.
The engine itself is pure NumPy and SciPy; ORE and QuantLib belong to the bake, never to the engine.

What the method is compared against, and its acceptance criterion, are fixed in the specification. The simulated single-swap expected exposure must match ORE within the Monte Carlo error at every grid point; the EEPE and the CVA recomputed from the expected exposure must match ORE; the convergence in the number of paths is reported. The closed forms are held to QuantLib 1.44 to a relative $10^{-6}$. The battery of the engine adds the identities of this subsection as rows: the analytic against the simulated expected exposure
on the reset dates within three standard errors, the martingale test of the discounted bonds within three standard errors, the EEPE and the CVA recomputed to a relative $10^{-9}$, the path convergence, the reconciliation with ORE within two combined standard errors, and the two backtests. These thresholds are internal acceptance criteria and not regulatory requirements.

\subsection{The standardised calculators: SA-CCR, BA-CVA, the output floor, SMA, LCR, NSFR and the FRTB sensitivities-based method}
\label{sec:m21}

\subsubsection{The standardised approach to counterparty credit risk}

SA-CCR replaces the simulation by a formula over the trades of a netting set \citep{ccr:cre52}. The exposure at default is
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
EAD&=\alpha\,(RC+PFE),\quad \alpha=1.4,\qquad PFE=\text{multiplier}\cdot AddOn^{\mathrm{agg}},\\
\text{multiplier}&=\min\Big\{1,\ \mathrm{Fl}+(1-\mathrm{Fl})\exp\Big(\frac{V-C}{2(1-\mathrm{Fl})\,AddOn^{\mathrm{agg}}}\Big)\Big\},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-sa}
\end{equation}
where $V$ is the netting-set value, $C$ the haircut value of the net collateral held, the variation margin plus the net independent collateral amount $NICA$ defined below (CRE52.10 and CRE52.17), $\mathrm{Fl}=5$ percent the floor of the multiplier, and $AddOn^{\mathrm{agg}}=\sum_aAddOn^{(a)}$ the sum over the five asset classes (interest rate, foreign exchange, credit, equity and commodity). The replacement cost is $RC=\max\{V-C,0\}$ for an
unmargined set and $RC=\max\{V-C,\ TH+MTA-NICA,\ 0\}$ for a margined set, with $TH$ the threshold, $MTA$ the minimum transfer amount and $NICA$ the net independent collateral amount, the collateral of the counterparty less the unsegregated collateral posted by the bank. The multiplier is 1 when $V-C\ge0$ and is below 1 when the netting set is out of the money
or over-collateralised, which credits the surplus. The supervisory duration of a trade running from $S$ to $E$ years and the maturity factors are
\begin{equation}
\begin{gathered}
SD=\frac{e^{-0.05S}-e^{-0.05E}}{0.05},\\
MF^{\mathrm{unmargined}}=\sqrt{\min\{\max\{M,\tfrac{10}{250}\},1\}},\qquad MF^{\mathrm{margined}}=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{MPoR}}{250}},
\end{gathered}
\label{eq:ccr-sd}
\end{equation}
with $M$ the residual maturity in years, floored at 10 business days (CRE52.48), and MPoR in business days. For an interest rate hedging set (a currency) the trades are allocated to maturity buckets by end date, B1 below one year, B2 from one to five years and B3 above five, and the effective notional of a trade is its supervisory delta times its adjusted notional ($N\cdot SD$) times the maturity factor;
with $D^{B1},D^{B2},D^{B3}$ the signed sums per bucket,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
EN_{HS}&=\sqrt{(D^{B1})^2+(D^{B2})^2+(D^{B3})^2+1.4\,D^{B1}D^{B2}+1.4\,D^{B2}D^{B3}+0.6\,D^{B1}D^{B3}},\\
AddOn_{HS}&=0.005\,EN_{HS},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-ir}
\end{equation}
or $|D^{B1}|+|D^{B2}|+|D^{B3}|$ when no offset is recognised. The other classes have their own aggregation. Foreign exchange sums $0.04\,|EN_{\text{pair}}|$ over currency pairs. For credit, equity and commodity the entity add-ons $A_e=SF_e\,EN_e$ combine with one correlation per entity,
\begin{equation}
AddOn=\Big[\Big(\sum_e\rho_e\,A_e\Big)^2+\sum_e(1-\rho_e^2)\,A_e^2\Big]^{1/2},
\label{eq:ccr-entity}
\end{equation}
where the engine takes $\rho_e$ per entity because credit and equity aggregate single names (correlation 0.5) and indices (0.8) in one formula. The supervisory factors of the Table of CRE52.72 are module data, each cell with its paragraph and in-force date: interest rate 0.5 percent; foreign exchange 4.0 percent; credit single name from 0.38 percent (AAA, AA) to
6.0 percent (CCC) and index 0.38 and 1.06 percent; equity single name 32 percent and index 20 percent; commodity electricity 40 percent and the other classes 18 percent. The supervisory delta of a linear trade is $\pm1$; for an option with price $P$, strike $K$, volatility $\sigma$ and time $T$ it is, for a bought call, $\Phi(d)$ with $d=\big(\ln(P/K)+\tfrac12\sigma^2T\big)/(\sigma\sqrt T)$,
and the sold call, the bought put and the sold put follow by sign and by $\Phi(-d)$; for a tranche between attachment $A$ and detachment $D$ it is $\pm15/\big((1+14A)(1+14D)\big)$.

The procedure for a netting set is Algorithm~\ref{alg:ccr-saccr}. On the book of C12 the interest rate hedging set is the only non-empty one. For the netting set the signed bucket sums are \ccrDOneNetting{}, \ccrDTwoNetting{} and \ccrDThreeNetting{} USD million in B1, B2 and B3, which combine by Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-ir} to an effective notional of \ccrENNetting{} USD million; the dominant term is the ten-year payer swap,
whose adjusted notional is the notional times a supervisory duration of \ccrSdTen{} years. A margined netting set uses the maturity factor of Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-sd}, which is \ccrMaturityFactorCsa{} at a margin period of 10 business days, so the add-on of a margined set is a fraction of the unmargined one, while the replacement cost carries the floor $TH+MTA-NICA$.

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{The SA-CCR exposure at default of a netting set from its trades (engine \texttt{regulatory.sa\_ccr}, cases of C12 and CRE99).}
\label{alg:ccr-saccr}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require trades with asset class, hedging set, start $S$, end $E$, notional, supervisory delta; $V$, $C$, $TH$, $MTA$, $NICA$; margined flag and MPoR; supervisory factors and correlations of CRE52.72
\For{each trade}
  \State compute $SD(S,E)$, the maturity factor of Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-sd} and the effective notional $\delta\cdot N\cdot SD\cdot MF$; assign the maturity bucket of an interest rate trade
\EndFor
\For{each asset class and hedging set}
  \State aggregate the effective notionals by Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-ir} (interest rate), the pair sum (foreign exchange) or Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-entity} (credit, equity, commodity); multiply by the supervisory factor
\EndFor
\State $AddOn^{\mathrm{agg}}\leftarrow\sum_a AddOn^{(a)}$; compute $RC$ (unmargined or margined form) and the multiplier by Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-sa}
\State $EAD\leftarrow1.4\,\big(RC+\text{multiplier}\cdot AddOn^{\mathrm{agg}}\big)$
\Ensure $RC$, every intermediate add-on, multiplier, $PFE$ and $EAD$ in one currency
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\subsubsection{The basic approach to CVA capital}

The capital for CVA risk in its basic reduced form is a diversified sum over counterparties of exposure weighted by a supervisory risk weight \citep{ccr:mar50},
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\text{capital}&=DS\cdot K_{\mathrm{reduced}},\qquad K_{\mathrm{reduced}}=\sqrt{\Big(\rho\sum_cSCVA_c\Big)^2+(1-\rho^2)\sum_cSCVA_c^2},\\
SCVA_c&=\frac{1}{\alpha}RW_c\sum_{NS}M_{NS}\,EAD_{NS}\,DF_{NS},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-bacva}
\end{equation}
with $DS=0.65$ the discount scalar, $\rho=50$ percent the correlation of the credit spreads of different counterparties, $\alpha=1.4$, $RW_c$ the risk weight of counterparty $c$ by sector and credit quality (the Table of MAR50.16: 0.5 percent for sovereigns, central banks and multilateral development banks of investment grade, 1.0 percent for local government, 5.0 percent for financials of investment grade, and up to 12.0 percent for
financials and other sectors of high yield), $M_{NS}$ the effective maturity of the netting set, $EAD_{NS}$ its exposure at default and $DF_{NS}=\big(1-e^{-0.05M_{NS}}\big)/(0.05M_{NS})$ the supervisory discount factor, equal to 1 for a bank that uses the internal model method. A bank with aggregate non-centrally-cleared derivative notional of EUR 100 billion or less may set CVA capital equal to its counterparty credit risk capital.
The full version blends the reduced form with a hedged form, $K_{\mathrm{full}}=\beta K_{\mathrm{reduced}}+(1-\beta)K_{\mathrm{hedged}}$ with $\beta=0.25$ and $K_{\mathrm{hedged}}$ built from the single-name and index hedges; the engine takes the hedge terms from the caller. With no hedges the hedged form equals the reduced form, so the full base equals $K_{\mathrm{reduced}}$; with perfect hedges ($K_{\mathrm{hedged}}=0$) it reaches its floor $\beta K_{\mathrm{reduced}}$, and $K_{\mathrm{full}}$ never falls below it. With one counterparty the reduced form is that
counterparty's $SCVA$, so the capital is $0.65\,SCVA$. In C12 the counterparty is a financial of investment grade, $RW=0.05$, the exposure is the SA-CCR exposure at default of the variant, and $M$ is the notional-weighted average maturity of the netting set, \ccrBaCvaM{} years for the book and \ccrBaCvaMSingle{} for the single swap. That reading of $M$ for a bank without the internal model method is not confirmed by the text of MAR50.15 that could be read and is unverified. No official numerical example of the basic approach was found in the sources read, so the tests rest on invariants: with $\rho=1$ the reduced base is the sum of the $SCVA_c$, and
the full base with no hedges is $K_{\mathrm{reduced}}$, the hedge-free value, and with perfect hedges it is $\beta K_{\mathrm{reduced}}$. The standardised approach to CVA, SA-CVA (MAR50.27 onward), is not implemented.

\subsubsection{The output floor}

The risk-weighted assets of a bank that uses internal models cannot fall below a share of the standardised requirement, and during the phase-in a national cap limits the increase \citep{ccr:rbc20,ccr:rbc90},
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
RWA&=\max\big(RWA_{\mathrm{nom}},\ f_t\,RWA_{\mathrm{SA}}\big),\qquad f_t=72.5\%\ \text{fully phased in},\\
RWA^{\mathrm{cap}}&=\min\big(RWA,\ RWA_{\mathrm{nom}}\,(1+c)\big),\qquad c=25\%,
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-floor}
\end{equation}
where $RWA_{\mathrm{nom}}$ are the risk-weighted assets of the approved approaches, $RWA_{\mathrm{SA}}$ those of the same exposures under the standardised approaches only, $f_t$ the phase-in factor and $c$ the optional national cap. The phase-in factor of RBC90.1 is \ccrPhaseInFirst{} in \ccrPhaseInFirstYear{} and \ccrPhaseInLast{} from 2028; the floor base excludes the internal ratings-based approach, the internal
models approach for market risk and the internal model method for counterparty credit risk. The BCBS dates are used where a jurisdiction passes none; the national schedules of the European Union, the United Kingdom and the United States are not modelled.

\subsubsection{The standardised measurement approach to operational risk}

The standardised approach to operational risk multiplies a business indicator component by an internal loss multiplier \citep{ccr:ope25},
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{ORC}&=\mathrm{BIC}\times\mathrm{ILM},\qquad \mathrm{ILM}=\ln\!\Big(e-1+\Big(\frac{LC}{\mathrm{BIC}}\Big)^{0.8}\Big),\\
\mathrm{BIC}&=0.12\min(BI,1)+0.15\big(\min(BI,30)-1\big)^{+}+0.18\,(BI-30)^{+},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-sma}
\end{equation}
with the business indicator $BI=\mathrm{ILDC}+\mathrm{SC}+\mathrm{FC}$ in EUR billion, $LC=15\times$ the average annual operational loss net of recoveries over the previous ten years, and the risk-weighted assets $12.5\times\mathrm{ORC}$. The interest, lease and dividend component is $\min(\overline{|II-IE|},2.25\%\,\overline{IEA})+\overline{DI}$, the services component $\max(\overline{OOI},\overline{OOE})+\max(\overline{FI},\overline{FE})$ and the
financial component $\overline{|\text{Net P\&L}_{TB}|}+\overline{|\text{Net P\&L}_{BB}|}$, where a bar is the three-year average and the absolute values of the net items are taken year by year before averaging. The multiplier is 1 exactly when the loss component equals the business indicator component and exceeds 1 when it is larger. The engine applies the rules of the standard in a fixed order: fewer than five years of loss data give a capital equal to the
business indicator component only, and never a multiplier computed on too little data; a national discretion may set the multiplier to 1; a bank in the first bucket has multiplier 1 unless losses are included by discretion; otherwise the multiplier is computed. The sensitivity of the multiplier to a single large loss is a property of the formula that critics of the approach stress \citep{ccr:peters2016}. The
definitions of the business indicator items were amended by a later publication whose content was not compared \citep{ccr:d610}, and the engine takes the items as inputs without applying those definitions.

\subsubsection{The liquidity coverage ratio and the net stable funding ratio}

The liquidity ratios compare a stock of liquid assets with stressed outflows over 30 days, and available with required stable funding over a year \citep{ccr:lcr,ccr:nsf}. The model of Diamond and Dybvig, in which a demand-deposit contract has a good equilibrium and a run equilibrium, is the conceptual explanation of the uninsured-deposit share as a run-risk driver \citep{ccr:diamond1983}; Contraste uses it as an explanation only and not as a calibrated component. The equations are
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
LCR&=\frac{HQLA}{NCO_{30d}}\ge100\%,\quad NCO=O-\min(I,\,0.75\,O),\\
HQLA&=L1+L2A+L2B-Adj_{15}-Adj_{40},\\
Adj_{15}&=\max\!\Big(L2B-\tfrac{15}{85}(L1+L2A),\ L2B-\tfrac{15}{60}L1,\ 0\Big),\\
Adj_{40}&=\max\!\Big(L2A+L2B-Adj_{15}-\tfrac23L1,\ 0\Big),\\
NSFR&=\frac{ASF}{RSF}\ge100\%,\quad ASF=\sum_jf^{ASF}_jL_j,\\
RSF&=\sum_if^{RSF}_iA_i+\sum_kf^{RSF}_kOBS_k+r\,D,
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-liq}
\end{equation}
where $O$ and $I$ are the stressed outflows and inflows of the 30 days, inflows counted up to 75 percent of outflows, $L1$, $L2A$ and $L2B$ the Level 1, Level 2A and Level 2B stocks after haircuts, $Adj_{15}$ and $Adj_{40}$ the adjustments that enforce the caps of 15 percent for Level 2B and 40 percent for Level 2, $f$ the factors of
the tables, $L_j$, $A_i$ and $OBS_k$ the funding, asset and off-balance-sheet amounts, $D$ the gross derivative liabilities and $r$ the add-on rate. The add-on rate is supplied by the caller within 5 to 20 percent and never defaulted, because the rule leaves the value to the supervisor, and the trade finance outflow rate is likewise a caller input. The module data hold the outflow and inflow rates, the haircuts and the funding factors, each key with its paragraph and the in-force date 15 December 2019.
No official worked example of the LCR or the NSFR exists, so none is claimed: the reference values are constructed from the formulas, the caps are checked on a grid of balance sheets and every table key against a copy of its source. A ratio below one under a stress scenario is not a breach, since the minimum applies in normal times, and a non-positive denominator is refused, never reported as an infinite ratio.

\subsubsection{The FRTB sensitivities-based method and the liquidity-horizon cascade}

The sensitivities-based method weights the sensitivities of a position to its risk factors and aggregates them within and across buckets, in three correlation scenarios \citep{ccr:mar21}. For a bucket $b$ with weighted sensitivities $WS_k=RW_ks_k$, risk weights $RW_k$ and within-bucket correlations $\rho_{kl}$, and for buckets with cross-bucket correlations $\gamma_{bc}$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
K_b&=\sqrt{\max\Big(0,\sum_kWS_k^2+\sum_k\sum_{l\ne k}\rho_{kl}WS_kWS_l\Big)},\qquad S_b=\sum_{k\in b}WS_k,\\
\text{charge}&=\sqrt{\max\Big(0,\sum_bK_b^2+\sum_b\sum_{c\ne b}\gamma_{bc}S_bS_c\Big)},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-sbm}
\end{equation}
and if the radicand of the second sum is negative then $S_b$ is replaced by $\max\big[\min\big(\sum_kWS_k,K_b\big),\,\allowbreak-K_b\big]$ for every bucket and the sum recomputed. The three scenarios scale the correlations, $\rho^{\mathrm{high}}=\min(1.25\rho,1)$ and $\rho^{\mathrm{low}}=\max(2\rho-1,0.75\rho)$, and the requirement is the largest charge over the scenarios. Only the general interest rate risk class (GIRR) is
parameterised, which is the class of a swap book. Its delta sensitivity is the change of value for a one basis point bump divided by 0.0001, $s_k=\big(V(r_k+0.0001)-V(r_k)\big)/0.0001$, which is not the value of a basis point; the tenors are 0.25 to 30 years, the risk weights 1.7 to 1.1 percent, and for a specified currency such as the US dollar the weights may be divided by $\sqrt2$ at the bank's discretion, which Contraste does in the headline charge and
labels as a convention, with the undivided charge beside it. The correlations of the ten tenors are the table of MAR21.46, reconstructed by $\rho_{kl}=\max\big(\exp[-0.03\,|T_k-T_l|/\min(T_k,T_l)],0.40\big)$ to the printed 0.1 percent, with 0.999 for the same tenor on another curve and $\gamma=0.5$ across buckets. Curvature, vega, the default risk charge and the other risk classes are out of scope.

The liquidity-horizon cascade of expected shortfall scales the shortfall of each group of risk factors by the length of its liquidity horizon \citep{ccr:mar33},
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
ES&=\sqrt{\big(ES_T(P)\big)^2+\sum_{j\ge2}\Big(ES_T(P,j)\sqrt{\frac{LH_j-LH_{j-1}}{T}}\Big)^2},\\
T&=10,\qquad LH_j=10,20,40,60,120\ \text{days},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:ccr-cascade}
\end{equation}
where $ES_T(P)$ is the shortfall of the whole portfolio over $T=10$ days and $ES_T(P,j)$ the shortfall obtained by shocking only the risk factors whose liquidity horizon is at least $LH_j$. The horizon of each risk factor class is module data with its paragraph.

\subsubsection{Parameters, procedure, complexity, implementation and acceptance}

Every parameter of the calculators is a transcribed regulatory constant and carries the paragraph, the table and the in-force date of the chapter version; none is estimated, and the caller supplies what the rules leave open: the margin period, the add-on rate of the NSFR, the trade finance rate, the hedge terms of BA-CVA and the phase-in factor of a jurisdiction. The procedure
of the central calculator is Algorithm~\ref{alg:ccr-saccr}; the others are direct evaluations of Equations~\ref{eq:ccr-bacva} to~\ref{eq:ccr-cascade}. The costs are linear or quadratic and small: SA-CCR is $O(T)$ for $T$ trades plus the cost of the hedging-set aggregation, BA-CVA is $O(C\,N)$ for $C$ counterparties with $N$ netting sets, the sensitivities-based aggregation is $O(K^2)$ per bucket for $K$ risk factors and $O(B^2)$ across $B$
buckets, and the output floor, the standardised measurement approach and the two liquidity ratios are $O(1)$ in the size of the inputs. These are derived orders from the formulas.

The implementation is \ccrfn{riskvalidation} 1.1.0: \ccrfn{riskvalidation.regulatory.sa_ccr}, \ccrfn{ba_cva}, \ccrfn{output_floor}, \ccrfn{frtb} and \ccrfn{lcr_nsfr}, and \ccrfn{riskvalidation.oprisk.sma}. Every function is pure and deterministic, never mutates its inputs and raises an error naming the field when an input is missing or invalid. The pipeline module \ccrfn{pipeline/cases/c12/regulatory.py} reads the fields of the SA-CCR, BA-CVA and GIRR calls
into the C12 documents, and the parity bake of the regulatory calculators writes the examples that follow. The acceptance criterion of the specification is that the official worked examples are reproduced (the five SA-CCR netting sets, the business indicator component of 5.37 billion for a business indicator of 35 billion, and the output floor values of 101.5 and 95) and that invariants hold for BA-CVA, the sensitivities-based method, the LCR and
the NSFR where no official example exists. The results of both tests are in Section~\ref{sec:results-ccr}.

\subsubsection{Calibration and the book}

Table~\ref{tab:ccr-book} lists the four swaps of the book, whose fixed rates are the par yields of \ccrCurveDate{} rounded to 10 basis points, and Table~\ref{tab:ccr-params} lists the parameters of the six variants. Figure~\ref{fig:ccr-calibration} shows the estimates of $a$ and $\sigma$ at each of the \ccrCalDates{} backtest dates. The mean reversion falls from \ccrCalFirstA{}
at the first date to \ccrHwA{} at the curve date as the window grows, and its standard error at the curve date, \ccrHwASe, is about half of the estimate; the volatility stays between \ccrCalSigmaMin{} and \ccrCalSigmaMax. The figure does not show that the model is right for the long end of the curve, only that the estimate of the speed is imprecise,
which Table~\ref{tab:ccr-sensitivity} converts into an exposure: moving $a$ by one standard error changes the EEPE of the netting set from \ccrEepeNetting{} USD to \ccrEepeAPlus{} USD at $a=\ccrAPlusValue$ (a change of \ccrEepeAPlusPct{} percent) or to \ccrEepeAMinus{} USD at $a=\ccrAMinusValue$ (\ccrEepeAMinusPct{} percent), while moving $\sigma$ by one standard error changes it by less than
\ccrEepeSigmaPct{} percent, from \ccrEepeNetting{} to \ccrEepeSigmaPlus{} and \ccrEepeSigmaMinus{} USD. The uncertainty of the exposure is thus driven by $a$, not by $\sigma$; Figure~\ref{fig:ccr-sensitivity} shows the shift of the whole profile.

\subsubsection{Exposure and CVA of the six variants}

Table~\ref{tab:ccr-exposure} and Figure~\ref{fig:ccr-ee-profiles} give the exposure measures. The single ten-year payer swap has an EEPE of \ccrEepeSingle{} USD (standard error \ccrEepeSeSingle) and a CVA of \ccrCvaDSingle{} USD (standard error \ccrCvaSeSingle). Netting with the other three swaps lowers the EEPE to \ccrEepeNetting{} USD, a cut of \ccrNettingCutEepe{} percent, and the CVA to \ccrCvaDNetting{} USD. At one year the sum of the single-trade expected exposures is
\ccrSumSingleOneYear{} USD and the netted one \ccrNettedOneYear{} USD, so netting removes \ccrNettingBenefitOneYear{} USD, \ccrNettingBenefitPct{} percent of the sum. The peak expected exposure is \ccrEePeakNetting{} USD in both variants and falls at \ccrPeakTimeNetting{} years, where the shorter swaps have matured and the book is the ten-year swap alone, so the two profiles coincide there; the
peak 95 percent PFE is \ccrPfePeakSingle{} USD for the single swap and \ccrPfePeakNetting{} USD for the netting set. The effective maturity is \ccrEffMaturity{} years in every variant, the cap of Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-eff}: the expected exposure beyond the first year is large relative to the effective expected exposure of the first year.

A credit support annex with a margin period of 10 business days lowers the EEPE to \ccrEepeCsaShort{} USD, \ccrCutCsaShort{} percent below the uncollateralised \ccrEepeNetting{} USD, and the CVA to \ccrCvaDCsaShort{} USD; with 20 business days the EEPE is \ccrEepeCsaLong{} USD, \ccrCutCsaLong{} percent lower, and the CVA \ccrCvaDCsaLong{} USD. The doubling of the period multiplies the EEPE by \ccrRatioLongShort. The
profile does not go to zero because of the lag: at one year the expected exposure is \ccrEeOneYearCsaShort{} USD with the short period and \ccrEeOneYearCsaLong{} USD with the long one. Adding the regression initial margin brings the EEPE to \ccrEepeIm{} USD (standard error \ccrEepeSeIm) and the CVA to \ccrCvaDIm{} USD. The margin is \ccrDimZero{} USD at the first report date and peaks at \ccrDimPeak{} USD, against
a peak variation-margin-only expected exposure of \ccrEeVmOnlyPeak{} USD, so the margin is several times the peak expected exposure after variation margin and what remains is a tail of paths. The figures say how large the exposure is under each convention; they do not say which convention a counterparty has, since the credit support annex is an assumption of the book.

\subsubsection{Wrong-way risk}

Table~\ref{tab:ccr-wwr} and Figure~\ref{fig:ccr-wwr} show the CVA of the netting set against $b$. At $b=0$ the CVA is \ccrWwrCvaZero{} USD, equal to the independent value of \ccrCvaWwrIndependent{} USD. It rises with $b$ at every step, to \ccrWwrCvaOne{} USD at $b=1$ (\ccrWwrPctOne{} percent more), \ccrWwrCvaTwo{} USD at $b=2$ (\ccrWwrPctTwo{} percent) and \ccrWwrCvaFour{} USD at $b=4$
(\ccrWwrPctFour{} percent, a factor of \ccrWwrRatioFour), and falls to \ccrWwrCvaNegTwo{} USD at $b=-2$, the right-way case (\ccrWwrPctNegTwo{} percent). The calibration error of $a(t)$ is at most $\ccrWwrMaxCalErr$, so the unconditional default probability is preserved to rounding. The largest portfolio value on the simulated paths is \ccrWwrWMax{} USD million, so the largest exponent $bw$ of the grid
is \ccrWwrMaxBw{}: the grid moves the hazard materially and is not a small perturbation. The result is conditional on the hazard model of Equation~\ref{eq:ccr-wwr}; it has no reconciliation with ORE, whose wrong-way example is a model with a correlated credit factor and not this one, and the choice of $b$ is the analyst's, which is why the sweep is shown.

\subsubsection{Regulatory measures beside the model}

Table~\ref{tab:ccr-regulatory} and Figure~\ref{fig:ccr-regulatory} put the measures side by side. For the netting set the SA-CCR exposure at default is \ccrEadNetting{} USD, against \ccrAlphaEepeNetting{} USD for $1.4$ times the EEPE, a ratio of \ccrRatioEadNetting; for the single swap the ratio is \ccrRatioEadSingle. The standardised measure is the larger for this book; its add-on of
\ccrAddOnNetting{} USD is set from notionals, maturities and supervisory factors and does not depend on the current value, and the multiplier of \ccrMultNetting{} (single swap \ccrMultSingle) credits only part of the out-of-the-money value of \ccrVNetting{} USD (Table~\ref{tab:ccr-saccr}). The EEPE under the stressed calibration of \ccrStressStart{} to \ccrStressEnd{} is \ccrStressedNetting{} USD, below the base EEPE of \ccrEepeNetting{} USD, although the Treasury corporate five-year spread rose
over the window from \ccrStressedSpreadStart{} to \ccrStressedSpreadPeak. A calibration window that contains a stress period therefore does not by itself produce a larger exposure for this book; the estimates of $a$ and $\sigma$ of that window are not exported in the artifacts, and the reason is not examined. With a credit support annex the SA-CCR exposure falls to \ccrEadCsaShort{} USD (10 days) and \ccrEadCsaLong{} USD (20 days), because
the margined maturity factor is \ccrMaturityFactorCsa{} at 10 days and the replacement cost floor is $TH+MTA-NICA=$ \ccrRcCsa{} USD; adding the initial margin lowers it to \ccrEadIm{} USD, a difference of \ccrEadCsaImDiff{} USD. The standard credits the initial margin through the net independent collateral amount in both places where the net collateral $C$ enters (CRE52.10, CRE52.17 and CRE52.23). In the replacement cost, the floor $TH+MTA-NICA$ becomes negative and the replacement cost falls from \ccrRcCsa{} to \ccrRcIm{} USD, which is $1.4$ times \ccrRcCsa{} USD, \ccrAlphaRcCsa{} USD of the difference. In the multiplier, $C$ is the variation margin plus the net independent collateral amount of \ccrNica{} USD, \ccrCIm{} USD against the netting-set value of \ccrVNetting{} USD, so the multiplier falls from 1 to \ccrMultIm{}, which accounts for the remaining \ccrEadMultDiff{} USD. The model, for its part, removes almost all of the expected exposure (EEPE \ccrEepeIm{} USD). BA-CVA capital is \ccrBaCvaSingle{} USD for the single swap and \ccrBaCvaNetting{} USD for the netting set, and \ccrBaCvaIm{} USD with initial margin. The GIRR delta charge with the weights divided by $\sqrt2$ is \ccrGirrSingle{} USD for the single swap and \ccrGirrNetting{} USD for the netting set, against
\ccrGirrUndividedNetting{} USD undivided for the netting set (Figure~\ref{fig:ccr-girr}); the same charge is reported for the margined variants because it depends on sensitivities and not on collateral. These figures describe a synthetic book; they say how the measures relate for one structure of trades and not that SA-CCR is generally above the model.

\subsubsection{Reconciliation with the reference engines}

Table~\ref{tab:ccr-ore} and Figure~\ref{fig:ccr-ore-gaps} compare the engine with ORE 1.8.17.0. For the two uncollateralised variants the expected exposure agrees with ORE at \ccrOreWithinSingle{} and \ccrOreWithinNetting{} of the \ccrOreGridPoints{} report dates within two combined standard errors, with a largest gap of \ccrOreGapSingle{} and \ccrOreGapNetting{} standard errors, and the EEPE and the CVA agree within \ccrOreEepeGapSingle{} and
\ccrOreCvaGapSingle{} standard errors for the single swap (ORE gives an EEPE of \ccrOreEepeSingle{} USD and a CVA of \ccrOreCvaSingle{} USD) and within \ccrOreEepeGapNetting{} and \ccrOreCvaGapNetting{} for the netting set (\ccrOreEepeNetting{} and \ccrOreCvaNetting{} USD).
\input{tables/ccr-t-ore}
For the collateralised variants they do not: \ccrOreWithinCsaShort{} and \ccrOreWithinCsaLong{} of the \ccrOreGridPoints{} dates agree, the largest expected-exposure gaps are \ccrOreGapCsaShort{} and \ccrOreGapCsaLong{} standard errors, and the CVA gaps are \ccrOreCvaGapCsaShort{} and \ccrOreCvaGapCsaLong{} standard errors, which are \ccrOreCvaRelCsaShort{} and \ccrOreCvaRelCsaLong{} percent of ORE's CVA. The failing dates are not scattered: the first is \ccrOreFirstFailCsaShort{} years for the short period and \ccrOreFirstFailCsaLong{} years for the long one, ORE's expected exposure is below the engine's from there, the gap deepens towards the 8.5 and 9 year dates (Figure~\ref{fig:ccr-ore-gaps}), and it reverses sign at the last report date, \ccrOreLastFailCsaShort{} years. The EEPE of the
two engines differs by \ccrOreEepeRelCsaShort{} and \ccrOreEepeRelCsaLong{} percent. With a minimum transfer amount of zero in both engines the largest gaps shrink to \ccrMtaZeroGapShort{} and \ccrMtaZeroGapLong{} standard errors and the rows remain outside two. For the variant with initial margin the expected exposure agrees at \ccrOreWithinIm{} of the \ccrOreGridPoints{} dates and fails only at the last, \ccrOreLastFailIm{} years, by \ccrOreGapIm{} standard errors, and ORE's mean dynamic initial margin is \ccrDimRatio{} of the engine's on average, a gap of \ccrDimGap{} combined standard errors. The two engines handle the margin differently: the engine applies the minimum transfer amount on the report grid, whereas ORE margins on its own call schedule, so its effect is larger in ORE. That this is the cause of the remaining gap, and the cause of the difference in the margin, is not
established by the artifacts. The reading that follows is limited: the engine and ORE agree for the uncollateralised exposure, which is the part that tests the Hull-White implementation, and disagree when collateral is added, by \ccrOreEepeRelCsaShort{} and \ccrOreEepeRelCsaLong{} percent of the EEPE for the two margin periods, by \ccrOreEepeRelIm{} percent for the variant with initial margin and by up to \ccrOreCvaRelCsaShort{} percent of the CVA; the artifacts attribute the disagreement to no single cause, and a different margin schedule is the candidate this paragraph names. The agreement of the uncollateralised profile does not
validate the margin logic.

\subsubsection{The exposure backtest}

Table~\ref{tab:ccr-backtest} and Figure~\ref{fig:ccr-backtest} give the backtest of the netting-set value and of the 3~month zero rate over \ccrBtDates{} dates. The model is rejected for the book value at all \ccrBtHorizons{} horizons: $W^2$ is \ccrBtWBookShort{} at 10 business days against a simulated 5 percent critical value of \ccrBtCritShort{} and a simulated 1 percent value of \ccrBtCritOneShort, and \ccrBtWBookLong{} at 12 months against \ccrBtCritLong{} and
\ccrBtCritOneLong. The critical values grow with the horizon as the effective sample size falls, from \ccrBtEssShort{} at 10 business days to \ccrBtEssLong{} at 12 months, but the statistic is above them at every horizon. The exceedances of the 95 percent PFE confirm it: \ccrBtExcTen{} in \ccrBtDates{} dates at 10 business days against \ccrBtExpected{} expected, \ccrBtExcTwenty{} at 20 business days, \ccrBtExcOne{} at one month, \ccrBtExcThree{} at three months, \ccrBtExcSix{} at six months
and \ccrBtExcTwelve{} at twelve months; at the 90 percent level the count at 10 business days is \ccrBtExcNinetyCount{} against \ccrBtExcNinetyExp{} and at the 99 percent level \ccrBtExcNinetyNineCount{} against \ccrBtExcNinetyNineExp. Because the horizons overlap these counts are not independent samples and are a secondary row.

\input{tables/ccr-t-backtest}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.98\textwidth]{ccr-backtest.pdf}
\caption{The Anderson-Darling statistic of the netting-set value and of the 3 month zero rate by horizon against the simulated 5 percent and 1 percent critical values (left, logarithmic axis), and the exceedances of the 95 percent PFE against the number expected (right), over the monthly dates of case C12.}
\label{fig:ccr-backtest}

The risk factor is rejected as well, with $W^2$ from \ccrBtWRfMin{} at the \ccrBtWRfMinHorizon{} horizon to \ccrBtWRfMax{} at the \ccrBtWRfMaxHorizon{} horizon, but its exceedances are fewer than expected at \ccrRfBelow{} of the \ccrBtHorizons{} horizons (between \ccrRfExcMin{} and \ccrRfExcMax{} against \ccrBtExpected{} expected), so the rejection of the 3~month rate does not come from too many exceedances. Figure~\ref{fig:ccr-pit} shows why the
two objects fail differently. The transforms of the book value at 10 business days are U-shaped: \ccrPitOuterBook{} percent of them fall in the two outer deciles where 20 percent are expected, which is the signature of a forecast distribution that is too narrow, and at 12 months \ccrPitLowBookYear{} percent fall in the lowest decile, so the realised value of the book is more often far below the simulated distribution than far above it. The transforms of the 3~month rate at 10 business days
are concentrated at the centre: \ccrPitCentralRf{} percent fall between 0.4 and 0.6 where 20 percent are expected, so the simulated rate distribution is too wide over a ten-day horizon. A distribution that is too wide for the short rate and too narrow for a ten-year swap book is not one error of scale applied to every output of the model.
\input{tables/ccr-t-subwindows}
The sub-windows of Table~\ref{tab:ccr-subwindows} show that the rejection is not an episode: the statistic at 10 business days is \ccrSubPre{} before 2008, \ccrSubMid{} from 2008 to 2019 and \ccrSubPost{} from 2020, and the smallest value in the table is \ccrSubMin, all far above the independent 5 percent value of \ccrIidFive{} (the artifact does not report simulated critical values for the sub-windows). At 10 business days the statistic is
largest before 2008, while at the 12 month horizon the two earlier windows are about equal. The reading that the long end is not described by a factor estimated on the short rate is unverified, since no second factor was fitted. What the backtest shows is that the exposure distribution of this model, calibrated as stated and applied to a par book, would not have passed the test of CRE53.33 on these curves. It does not show how a
bank's own model, calibration and portfolio would perform.

\subsubsection{The standardised calculators against the published examples}

Table~\ref{tab:ccr-cre99} reproduces the five official SA-CCR examples from their trades: the exposure at default rounds to the published integer in \ccrCreExact{} of \ccrCreSets{} sets, with every intermediate value held to a relative \ccrCreTol. The unrounded exposures are \ccrCreEadOne{} for set 1 and \ccrCreEadFive{} for set 5, in USD thousands; the multiplier is \ccrCreMultTwo{} for set 2 and \ccrCreMultFive{} for set 5, against the printed
0.965 and 0.958, and the supervisory delta of the swaption of set 1 is \ccrCreDelta. The path from the printed rounded intermediates holds to one unit of the published exposure and not exactly, which is why the engine carries the unrounded add-ons. Table~\ref{tab:ccr-other} lists the other calculators: the business indicator component is \ccrSmaBic{} billion EUR for a business indicator of 35 billion, with \ccrSmaBicHalf{} and
\ccrSmaBicThirty{} at 0.5 and 30 billion, and the risk-weighted assets are \ccrSmaRwa{} billion; the output floor gives \ccrFloorValue{} and \ccrFloorCapped{} for the two examples of the standard; the sensitivities-based fallback charge is \ccrFallbackCharge{} and the liquidity cascade \ccrCascadeEs{}; the stock of high-quality liquid assets is \ccrHqlaOne{} with a Level 2B adjustment of \ccrHqlaAdjFifteen{} and \ccrHqlaTwo{} with a Level 2
adjustment of \ccrHqlaAdjForty. All \ccrOtherRows{} rows agree to a relative difference of at most $\ccrOtherWorst$, and the \ccrInvariantHold{} of \ccrInvariantRows{} invariant cases hold. For the calculators without an official example, BA-CVA, the sensitivities-based method, the LCR and the NSFR, the agreement is with values constructed from the same formulas, so it checks the implementation of the equations and not the
equations themselves, and it confirms nothing about a bank's reported ratio.
